claim: Xenoturbella bocki is a morphologically simple marine worm first described from specimens collected from muddy sediments in the Gullmarsfjord on the west coast of Sweden.
source: Xenoturbella bocki (Figure 1) is a morphologically simple marine worm first described from specimens collected from muddy sediments in the Gullmarsfjord on the west coast of Sweden.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the manuscript describing the species and its collection location.

claim: There are now six described species of Xenoturbella.
source: There are now six described species of Xenoturbella – the only genus in the higher-level taxon of Xenoturbellida (Telford, 2008).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the number of described species, supported by a citation.

claim: X. bocki was initially included as a species within the Platyhelminthes.
source: X. bocki was initially included as a species within the Platyhelminthes (Westblad, 1949), but molecular phylogenetic studies have shown that Xenoturbellida is the sister group of the Acoelomorpha, a second clade of morphologically simple worms also originally considered Platyhelminthes: Xenoturbellida and Acoelomorpha constitute their own phylum, the Xenacoelomorpha (Philippe et al., 2019; Cannon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a historical citation to Westblad, 1949.

claim: Molecular phylogenetic studies have shown that Xenoturbellida is the sister group of the Acoelomorpha.
source: X. bocki was initially included as a species within the Platyhelminthes (Westblad, 1949), but molecular phylogenetic studies have shown that Xenoturbellida is the sister group of the Acoelomorpha, a second clade of morphologically simple worms also originally considered Platyhelminthes: Xenoturbellida and Acoelomorpha constitute their own phylum, the Xenacoelomorpha (Philippe et al., 2019; Cannon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to molecular phylogenetic studies.

claim: Xenoturbellida and Acoelomorpha constitute their own phylum, the Xenacoelomorpha.
source: X. bocki was initially included as a species within the Platyhelminthes (Westblad, 1949), but molecular phylogenetic studies have shown that Xenoturbellida is the sister group of the Acoelomorpha, a second clade of morphologically simple worms also originally considered Platyhelminthes: Xenoturbellida and Acoelomorpha constitute their own phylum, the Xenacoelomorpha (Philippe et al., 2019; Cannon et al., 2016).
evidence: This taxonomic classification is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Xenacoelomorpha is convincingly supported by classical analysis in the field of evolution of development, including their sharing unique amino acid signatures in their Caudal genes.
source: In addition to multiple phylogenetic studies that support the monophyly of the phylum, Xenacoelomorpha is convincingly supported by classical analysis in the field of evolution of development, for example, their sharing unique amino acid signatures in their Caudal genes (Philippe et al., 2019) and a Hox4/5/6 gene (Ueki et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies on developmental evolution.

claim: Xenacoelomorpha share a Hox4/5/6 gene.
source: In addition to multiple phylogenetic studies that support the monophyly of the phylum, Xenacoelomorpha is convincingly supported by classical analysis in the field of evolution of development, for example, their sharing unique amino acid signatures in their Caudal genes (Philippe et al., 2019) and a Hox4/5/6 gene (Ueki et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ueki et al., 2019.

claim: A majority of studies have supported a position for Xenacoelomorpha as the sister group of all other Bilateria (the Protostomia and Deuterostomia, collectively named Nephrozoa).
source: There are two broadly discussed scenarios: a majority of studies have supported a position for Xenacoelomorpha as the sister group of all other Bilateria (the Protostomia and Deuterostomia, collectively named Nephrozoa) (Jimenez-Guri et al., 2006; Ryan et al., 2006; Jékely, 2013); work we have contributed to Telford, 2008; Philippe et al., 2019; Philippe et al., 2011; Bourlat et al., 2006, has instead placed Xenacoelomorpha within the Bilateria as the sister group of the Ambulacraria (Hemichordata and Echinodermata) to form a clade called the Xenambulacraria (Philippe et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Some work has placed Xenacoelomorpha within the Bilateria as the sister group of the Ambulacraria to form a clade called the Xenambulacraria.
source: There are two broadly discussed scenarios: a majority of studies have supported a position for Xenacoelomorpha as the sister group of all other Bilateria (the Protostomia and Deuterostomia, collectively named Nephrozoa) (Jimenez-Guri et al., 2006; Ryan et al., 2006; Jékely, 2013); work we have contributed to Telford, 2008; Philippe et al., 2019; Philippe et al., 2011; Bourlat et al., 2006, has instead placed Xenacoelomorpha within the Bilateria as the sister group of the Ambulacraria (Hemichordata and Echinodermata) to form a clade called the Xenambulacraria (Philippe et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies proposing this phylogenetic position.

claim: X. bocki has neither organized gonads nor a centralized nervous system.
source: X. bocki has neither organized gonads nor a centralized nervous system.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the morphological characteristics of X. bocki.

claim: X. bocki has a blind gut, no body cavities, and lacks nephrocytes.
source: It has a blind gut, no body cavities, and lacks nephrocytes (Nakano, 2015).
evidence: This morphological description is supported by a citation.

claim: The loss or remodeling of morphological complexity is a common feature of evolution in many animal groups and is typically associated with unusual modes of living.
source: The loss or remodeling of morphological complexity is a common feature of evolution in many animal groups and is typically associated with unusual modes of living (Martynov et al., 2020; Westheide, 1987) – in particular, the adoption of a sessile (sea squirts, barnacles) or parasitic (neodermatan flatworms, orthonectids) lifestyle, extreme miniaturization (e.g., tardigrades, orthonectids), or even neoteny (e.g., flightless hexapods).
evidence: This general evolutionary principle is supported by citations and examples.

claim: The common ancestor of the protostomes and deuterostomes has been reconstructed with approximately eight Hox genes.
source: For example, the common ancestor of the protostomes and deuterostomes has been reconstructed with approximately eight Hox genes but only four have been found in the Acoelomorpha (Nemertoderma) and five in Xenoturbella.
evidence: This is a statement about ancestral reconstruction based on comparative genomics.

claim: Only four Hox genes have been found in the Acoelomorpha (Nemertoderma).
source: For example, the common ancestor of the protostomes and deuterostomes has been reconstructed with approximately eight Hox genes but only four have been found in the Acoelomorpha (Nemertoderma) and five in Xenoturbella.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the number of Hox genes found in Acoelomorpha.

claim: Five Hox genes have been found in Xenoturbella.
source: For example, the common ancestor of the protostomes and deuterostomes has been reconstructed with approximately eight Hox genes but only four have been found in the Acoelomorpha (Nemertoderma) and five in Xenoturbella.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the number of Hox genes found in Xenoturbella.

claim: Analysis of the microRNAs (miRNAs) of an acoelomorph, Symsagittifera roscoffensis, found that many bilaterian miRNAs were absent from its genome.
source: Similarly, analysis of the microRNAs (miRNAs) of an acoelomorph, Symsagittifera roscoffensis, found that many bilaterian miRNAs were absent from its genome (Sempere et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Some of the missing bilaterian miRNAs were subsequently observed in Xenoturbella.
source: Some of the missing bilaterian miRNAs, however, were subsequently observed in Xenoturbella (Philippe et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Philippe et al., 2011.

claim: The analyses of gene content of Hofstenia showed similar numbers of genes and gene families to other bilaterians.
source: The analyses of gene content of Hofstenia showed similar numbers of genes and gene families to other bilaterians (Gehrke et al., 2019), while an analysis of the neuropeptide content concluded that most bilaterian neuropeptides were present in Xenacoelomorpha (Moroz et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gehrke et al., 2019.

claim: An analysis of the neuropeptide content concluded that most bilaterian neuropeptides were present in Xenacoelomorpha.
source: The analyses of gene content of Hofstenia showed similar numbers of genes and gene families to other bilaterians (Gehrke et al., 2019), while an analysis of the neuropeptide content concluded that most bilaterian neuropeptides were present in Xenacoelomorpha (Moroz et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moroz et al., 2021.

claim: The X. bocki genome assembly has a size of ~111 Mbp in 18 chromosome-like scaffolds.
source: Our highly contiguous genome assembly of X. bocki has a size of ~111 Mbp in 18 chromosome-like scaffolds, with repeat content and intron, exon, and intergenic space comparable to other bilaterian invertebrates.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genome assembly characteristics.

claim: The X. bocki genome has repeat content and intron, exon, and intergenic space comparable to other bilaterian invertebrates.
source: Our highly contiguous genome assembly of X. bocki has a size of ~111 Mbp in 18 chromosome-like scaffolds, with repeat content and intron, exon, and intergenic space comparable to other bilaterian invertebrates.
evidence: This comparative statement is based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: X. bocki has a similar number of genes to other bilaterians.
source: We find X. bocki to have a similar number of genes to other bilaterians and to have retained ancestral metazoan synteny.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the gene count analysis.

claim: X. bocki has retained ancestral metazoan synteny.
source: We find X. bocki to have a similar number of genes to other bilaterians and to have retained ancestral metazoan synteny.
evidence: This claim is based on synteny analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Key bilaterian signaling pathways are largely complete in X. bocki.
source: Key bilaterian signaling pathways are also largely complete and most bilaterian miRNAs are present.
evidence: This claim is based on the KEGG pathway analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most bilaterian miRNAs are present in X. bocki.
source: Key bilaterian signaling pathways are also largely complete and most bilaterian miRNAs are present.
evidence: This claim is based on the miRNA analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: X. bocki has a complex genome typical of bilaterians.
source: Overall, we conclude that X. bocki has a complex genome typical of bilaterians, which does not reflect the apparent simplicity of its body plan that has been so important to proposals that the Xenacoelomorpha are the simple sister group of the rest of the Bilateria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive genomic analysis.

claim: The X. bocki genome does not reflect the apparent simplicity of its body plan.
source: Overall, we conclude that X. bocki has a complex genome typical of bilaterians, which does not reflect the apparent simplicity of its body plan that has been so important to proposals that the Xenacoelomorpha are the simple sister group of the rest of the Bilateria.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the genomic data.

claim: The scaffolded genome has a span of 111 Mbp and an N50 of 2.7 Mbp.
source: The scaffolded genome has a span of 111 Mbp (117 Mbp including small fragments unincorporated into the HiC assembly) and an N50 of 2.7 Mbp (for contigs >500 bp).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genome assembly metrics.

claim: The assembly contains 18 megabase-scale scaffolds encompassing 72 Mbp (62%) of the genomic sequence, with 43% GC content.
source: The assembly contains 18 megabase-scale scaffolds encompassing 72 Mbp (62%) of the genomic sequence, with 43% GC content.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genome assembly characteristics.

claim: The original assembly indicated a repeat content of about 25% after a RepeatModeller-based RepeatMasker annotation.
source: The original assembly indicated a repeat content of about 25% after a RepeatModeller-based RepeatMasker annotation ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct statement about the repeat content analysis.

claim: About 2/3 of the repeats are not classified.
source: As often seen in non-model organisms, about 2/3 of the repeats are not classified.
evidence: This is a statement about the classification status of repeats.

claim: BRAKER predicted 15,154 gene models.
source: We used BRAKER (Hoff et al., 2019, Hoff et al., 2016) with extensive RNA-seq data, and additional single-cell UTR enriched transcriptome sequencing data to predict 15,154 gene models.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the gene prediction results.

claim: A total of 9575 gene models (63%) are found on the 18 large scaffolds.
source: A total of 9575 gene models (63%) are found on the 18 large scaffolds (which represent 62% of the total sequence).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the distribution of gene models.

claim: A total of 13,298 of the predicted genes (88%) have RNA-seq support.
source: A total of 13,298 of our predicted genes (88%) have RNA-seq support.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the RNA-seq support for gene predictions.

claim: The predicted X. bocki genes have a median coding length of 873 nt and a mean length of 1330 nt.
source: The predicted X. bocki genes have a median coding length of 873 nt and a mean length of 1330 nt.
evidence: This is a direct statement about gene length statistics.

claim: Median exon length is 132 nt (mean 212 nt) and median intron length is 131 nt (mean 394 nt).
source: Median exon length is 132 nt (mean 212 nt) and median intron length is 131 nt (mean 394 nt).
evidence: This is a direct statement about exon and intron length statistics.

claim: Genes have a median of 4 exons and a mean of 8.5 exons.
source: Genes have a median of 4 exons and a mean of 8.5 exons.
evidence: This is a direct statement about exon number statistics.

claim: A total of 2532 genes have a single exon, of which 1381 are supported as having a single exon by RNA-seq (TPM > 1).
source: A total of 2532 genes have a single exon, of which 1381 are supported as having a single exon by RNA-seq (TPM > 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about single-exon genes.

claim: X. bocki falls within the range of other similarly sized metazoan genomes for exon, intron, and intergenic sequence content.
source: A comparison of the exon, intron, and intergenic sequence content in Xenoturbella with those described in other animal genomes (Francis and Wörheide, 2017) shows that X. bocki falls within the range of other similarly sized metazoan genomes (Figure 2) for all these measures.
evidence: This comparative statement is based on the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The bacterial genome was found as five contigs spanning 1,906,303 bp (N50 of 1,237,287 bp), which were assembled into two large scaffolds.
source: The bacterial genome was found as five contigs spanning 1,906,303 bp (N50 of 1,237,287 bp), which were assembled into two large scaffolds.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the bacterial genome assembly.

claim: Using PROKKA, 1738 genes were predicted in the bacterial genome, with 3 ribosomal RNAs, 35 transfer RNAs, and 1 transfer-messenger RNA.
source: Using PROKKA (Seemann, 2014), we predicted 1738 genes in this bacterial genome, with 3 ribosomal RNAs, 35 transfer RNAs, and 1 transfer-messenger RNA.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the bacterial gene prediction results.

claim: The bacterial genome is 97.5% complete for bacterial BUSCO genes, missing only one of the 40 core genes.
source: The genome is 97.5% complete for bacterial BUSCO (Simão et al., 2015) genes, missing only one of the 40 core genes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the BUSCO completeness of the bacterial genome.

claim: The X. bocki-hosted Chlamydia belong to a group designated as Simkaniaceae.
source: The X. bocki-hosted Chlamydia belong to a group designated as Simkaniaceae in Dharamshi et al., 2020, with the sister taxon in our phylogenetic tree being the Chlamydia species previously found in X. westbladi (X. westbladi is almost certainly a synonym of X. bocki) (Rouse et al., 2016; Figure 3).
evidence: This phylogenetic placement is based on the analysis shown in Figure 3 and cited literature.

claim: The sister taxon to the X. bocki-hosted Chlamydia is the Chlamydia species previously found in X. westbladi.
source: The X. bocki-hosted Chlamydia belong to a group designated as Simkaniaceae in Dharamshi et al., 2020, with the sister taxon in our phylogenetic tree being the Chlamydia species previously found in X. westbladi (X. westbladi is almost certainly a synonym of X. bocki) (Rouse et al., 2016; Figure 3).
evidence: This phylogenetic relationship is shown in Figure 3.

claim: X. westbladi is almost certainly a synonym of X. bocki.
source: The X. bocki-hosted Chlamydia belong to a group designated as Simkaniaceae in Dharamshi et al., 2020, with the sister taxon in our phylogenetic tree being the Chlamydia species previously found in X. westbladi (X. westbladi is almost certainly a synonym of X. bocki) (Rouse et al., 2016; Figure 3).
evidence: This taxonomic interpretation is supported by a citation.

claim: The relationship between X. bocki and the Chlamydia is likely to be commensal or parasitic rather than a true symbiosis.
source: We found only slightly higher completeness in a small number of pathways involved in carbohydrate metabolism, carbon fixation, and amino acid metabolism (see supplementary material), suggesting that the relationship is likely to be commensal or parasitic rather than a true symbiosis.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the metabolic pathway analysis.

claim: 56 potential horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events were detected in the X. bocki genome.
source: We were able to detect 56 potential horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the HGT analysis results.

claim: One of the 56 HGT candidate genes is of chlamydial origin and thus likely originating from a bacterial contig.
source: Phylogenies generated using closest blast hits for each HGT candidate unveiled one of the 56 genes to be of chlamydial origin and thus likely originating from a bacterial contig.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of HGT candidates.

claim: 0.35% of the X. bocki genes might be horizontally acquired.
source: In summary, 0.35% of the X. bocki genes we have identified might be horizontally acquired.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the HGT analysis.

claim: In both phylogenetic analyses of gene presence/absence data, the best tree grouped Xenoturbella with the Ambulacraria.
source: In both analyses, the best tree grouped Xenoturbella with the Ambulacraria (Figure 4a).
evidence: This phylogenetic result is shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The analysis including acoels placed the acoels as the sister group to Nephrozoa separate from Xenoturbella.
source: The analysis including acoels, however, placed the acoels as the sister group to Nephrozoa separate from Xenoturbella (Figure 4b).
evidence: This phylogenetic result is shown in Figure 4b.

claim: For the Metazoa gene set in BUSCO (v5) the X. bocki proteome is 82.5% complete and ~90% complete when partial hits are included.
source: We found that for the Metazoa gene set in BUSCO (v5) the X. bocki proteome translated from our gene predictions is 82.5% complete and ~90% complete when partial hits are included (82 and 93%, respectively, for the Eukaryote gene set).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the BUSCO completeness analysis.

claim: The acoel H. miamia is 95.71% complete for the BUSCO Metazoa gene set.
source: This estimate is even higher in the acoel H. miamia, which was originally reported to be 90% (Gehrke et al., 2019), but in our re-analysis was 95.71%.
evidence: This is a re-analysis result comparing to the original report.

claim: The morphologically highly simplified and fast-evolving annelid Intoshia linei has a genome of fewer than 10,000 genes and is only ~64% complete for the BUSCO (v5) Metazoa set.
source: In comparison, the morphologically highly simplified and fast-evolving annelid Intoshia linei (Schiffer et al., 2018) has a genome of fewer than 10,000 genes (Mikhailov et al., 2016) and in our analysis is only ~64% complete for the BUSCO (v5) Metazoa set.
evidence: This comparative statement is based on BUSCO analysis and cited literature.

claim: The model nematode Caenorhabditis elegans is ~79% complete for the BUSCO Metazoa set.
source: The model nematode Caenorhabditis elegans is ~79% complete for the same set.
evidence: This is a comparative BUSCO analysis result.

claim: The average number of bilaterian genes present in bilaterians is 7577.
source: The average numbers of these genes present in bilaterians = 7577; Xenoturbella = 5459; Hofstenia = 5438; Praesagittifera = 4280; Drosophila = 4844 and Caenorhabditis = 4323.
evidence: This is a summary of the gene presence analysis.

claim: Xenoturbella has 5459 bilaterian genes present.
source: The average numbers of these genes present in bilaterians = 7577; Xenoturbella = 5459; Hofstenia = 5438; Praesagittifera = 4280; Drosophila = 4844 and Caenorhabditis = 4323.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the gene presence analysis.

claim: Hofstenia has 5438 bilaterian genes present.
source: The average numbers of these genes present in bilaterians = 7577; Xenoturbella = 5459; Hofstenia = 5438; Praesagittifera = 4280; Drosophila = 4844 and Caenorhabditis = 4323.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the gene presence analysis.

claim: The proportion of orthogroups containing an X. bocki protein is 87.4%.
source: The proportion of orthogroups containing an X. bocki and X. profunda protein (87.4 and 89.2%) are broadly similar to the proportions seen in other well-characterized genomes, for example, S. purpuratus proteins (93.8%) or N. vectensis proteins (84.3%) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the orthology analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The proportion of orthogroups containing an X. profunda protein is 89.2%.
source: The proportion of orthogroups containing an X. bocki and X. profunda protein (87.4 and 89.2%) are broadly similar to the proportions seen in other well-characterized genomes, for example, S. purpuratus proteins (93.8%) or N. vectensis proteins (84.3%) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the orthology analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both Xenoturbella species have an intermediate number of unassigned genes of ~11–12%.
source: Both Xenoturbella species have an intermediate number of unassigned genes of ~11–12%.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the orthology analysis.

claim: The proportion of species-specific genes in Xenoturbella is ~14% of all genes.
source: Similarly, the proportion of species-specific genes (~14% of all genes) corresponds closely to what is seen in most other species (with the exception of the parasitic annelid I. linei, Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about species-specific genes shown in Figure 5.

claim: 867 orthogroups are specific to the two Xenoturbella species.
source: In order to identify sets of orthologs specific to the two Xenoturbella species, we used the kinfin software (Laetsch and Blaxter, 2017a) and found 867 such groups in the OrthoFinder clustering.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the Xenoturbella-specific orthology analysis.

claim: The X. bocki gene set is largely complete in regard to the core proteins of cell signaling pathways.
source: The X. bocki gene set is largely complete in regard to the core proteins of these pathways, while an array of effector proteins is absent (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on the KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Xenoturbella is not significantly less complete in KEGG pathway completeness compared to other bilaterians considered to have low morphological complexity.
source: Xenoturbella is, however, not significantly less complete compared to other bilaterians considered to have low morphological complexity and which have been shown to have reduced gene content, such as C. elegans, the annelid parasite I. linei, or the acoel H. miamia (Figure 6).
evidence: This comparative statement is based on the KEGG analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Clear evidence of a syntenic Hox cluster with four Hox genes (centHox1, postHox, centHox3, and antHox1) was identified in the X. bocki genome.
source: We identified clear evidence of a syntenic Hox cluster with four Hox genes (centHox1, postHox, centHox3, and antHox1) in the X. bocki genome (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on the genomic analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: There was evidence of a fragmented annotation of centHox2, split between the four gene Hox cluster and a separate scaffold.
source: There was also evidence of a fragmented annotation of centHox2, split between the four gene Hox cluster and a separate scaffold (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on the genomic analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: All five Hox genes form a Hox cluster in the X. bocki genome, but there are possible unresolved assembly errors disrupting the current annotation.
source: In summary, this suggests that all five Hox genes form a Hox cluster in the X. bocki genome, but that there are possible unresolved assembly errors disrupting the current annotation.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the genomic data.

claim: Cdx and a new Gsx annotation were identified on the same scaffold.
source: We identified Cdx and a new Gsx annotation on the same scaffold, as well as a previously reported Gsx paralog on a separate scaffold.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the ParaHox gene identification.

claim: This indicates partial retention of the ParaHox cluster in X. bocki along with a duplication of Gsx.
source: This indicates partial retention of the ParaHox cluster in X. bocki along with a duplication of Gsx.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the ParaHox gene analysis.

claim: The homeobox genes of the pharyngeal cluster (Msxlx, Nk2-1/2/4/8) were present on a single X. bocki scaffold.
source: The homeobox genes of this cluster (Msxlx, Nk2-1/2/4/8) were present on a single X. bocki scaffold.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the pharyngeal cluster gene identification.

claim: 12 additional neuropeptide genes and 39 new neuropeptide receptors were discovered in X. bocki.
source: We have discovered 12 additional neuropeptide genes and 39 new neuropeptide receptors in X. bocki adding 6 bilaterian peptidergic systems to the Xenoturbella catalog (NPY-F; MCH/Asta-C; TRH; ETH; CCHa/Nmn-B; Np-S/CCAP), and 6 additional bilaterian systems to the Xenacoelomorpha catalog (Corazonin; Kiss/GPR54; GPR83; 7B2; Trunk/PTTH; NUCB2), making a total of 31 peptidergic systems (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the neuropeptide discovery shown in Figure 8.

claim: 6 bilaterian peptidergic systems were added to the Xenoturbella catalog (NPY-F; MCH/Asta-C; TRH; ETH; CCHa/Nmn-B; Np-S/CCAP).
source: We have discovered 12 additional neuropeptide genes and 39 new neuropeptide receptors in X. bocki adding 6 bilaterian peptidergic systems to the Xenoturbella catalog (NPY-F; MCH/Asta-C; TRH; ETH; CCHa/Nmn-B; Np-S/CCAP), and 6 additional bilaterian systems to the Xenacoelomorpha catalog (Corazonin; Kiss/GPR54; GPR83; 7B2; Trunk/PTTH; NUCB2), making a total of 31 peptidergic systems (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the neuropeptide systems identified.

claim: 6 additional bilaterian systems were added to the Xenacoelomorpha catalog (Corazonin; Kiss/GPR54; GPR83; 7B2; Trunk/PTTH; NUCB2).
source: We have discovered 12 additional neuropeptide genes and 39 new neuropeptide receptors in X. bocki adding 6 bilaterian peptidergic systems to the Xenoturbella catalog (NPY-F; MCH/Asta-C; TRH; ETH; CCHa/Nmn-B; Np-S/CCAP), and 6 additional bilaterian systems to the Xenacoelomorpha catalog (Corazonin; Kiss/GPR54; GPR83; 7B2; Trunk/PTTH; NUCB2), making a total of 31 peptidergic systems (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the neuropeptide systems identified.

claim: A total of 31 peptidergic systems were identified in X. bocki.
source: We have discovered 12 additional neuropeptide genes and 39 new neuropeptide receptors in X. bocki adding 6 bilaterian peptidergic systems to the Xenoturbella catalog (NPY-F; MCH/Asta-C; TRH; ETH; CCHa/Nmn-B; Np-S/CCAP), and 6 additional bilaterian systems to the Xenacoelomorpha catalog (Corazonin; Kiss/GPR54; GPR83; 7B2; Trunk/PTTH; NUCB2), making a total of 31 peptidergic systems (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary statement about the total neuropeptide systems.

claim: A very specific 'K/R-RFP-K/R' signature is shared only by ambulacrarian and X. bocki Prokineticin ligand sequences.
source: Our alignment reveals clade-specific signatures already reported in Ecdysozoa and Chordata sequences, but also two new signatures specific to Lophotrochozoa and Cnidaria sequences, as well as a very specific 'K/R-RFP-K/R' signature shared only by ambulacrarian and X. bocki sequences.
evidence: This is based on the sequence alignment analysis of Prokineticin ligands.

claim: The shared Ambulacrarian/Xenacoelomorpha signature is found at the same position as the Chordate sequence involved in receptor activation.
source: The shared Ambulacrarian/Xenacoelomorpha signature is found at the same position as the Chordate sequence involved in receptor activation – adjacent to the N-terminus of the Prokineticin domain (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on the sequence alignment shown in Figure 8.

claim: By deep sequencing two independent small RNA samples, 23 out of 31 bilaterian microRNA families were found in X. bocki.
source: By deep sequencing two independent small RNA samples, we have now identified the majority of the missing metazoan and bilaterian microRNAs and identified them in the genome assembly (Figure 9). Altogether, we found 23 out of 31 bilaterian microRNA families (35 genes including duplicates); the single known Metazoan microRNA family (MIR-10) in two copies; the Deuterostome-specific MIR-103; and 7 Xenoturbella-specific microRNAs, giving a total of 46 microRNA genes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the miRNA discovery shown in Figure 9.

claim: A total of 46 microRNA genes were identified in X. bocki.

claim: None of the protostome-specific miRNAs were found in X. bocki.
source: None of the protostome-specific miRNAs were found.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the absence of protostome-specific miRNAs.

claim: 24 ancestral linkage units are broadly preserved in bilaterians.
source: The availability of chromosome-scale genomes has made it possible to reconstruct 24 ancestral linkage units broadly preserved in bilaterians (Simakov et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited research on ancestral linkage groups.

claim: X. bocki has retained most of the ancestral bilaterian linkage units.
source: We compared the genome of Xenoturbella to several other metazoan genomes and found that it has retained most of these ancestral bilaterian units: 12 chromosomes in the X. bocki genome derive from a single ALG, 5 chromosomes are made of the fusion of 2 ALGs, and 1 Xenoturbella chromosome is a fusion of 3 ALGs, as highlighted with the comparison of ortholog content with amphioxus, the sea urchin, and the sea scallop (Figure 10 and supplementary material).
evidence: This is based on the synteny analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: The smallest of the 18 large scaffolds in the X. bocki genome did not show strong 1:1 clustering with any scaffold/chromosome of the bilaterian species compared.
source: The smallest of the 18 large scaffolds in the X. bocki genome did not show strong 1:1 clustering with any scaffold/chromosome of the bilaterian species we compared it to.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the aberrant scaffold analysis.

claim: Genes on the aberrant scaffold show a different age structure compared to other scaffolds, with both more older genes (pre bilaterian) and more Xenoturbella-specific genes.
source: In line with this, genes on the scaffold show a different age structure compared to other scaffolds, with both more older genes (pre bilaterian) and more Xenoturbella-specific genes (Figure 11; supported by Ks statistics, supplementary material).
evidence: This is based on the gene age analysis shown in Figure 11.

claim: The aberrant scaffold had significantly lower levels of methylation than the rest of the genome.
source: This aberrant scaffold also had significantly lower levels of methylation than the rest of the genome.
evidence: This is based on the methylation analysis.

claim: While Xenoturbella is generally described as having a very simple body, its genome is of a similar complexity to many other bilaterians.
source: Our data suggest that, while Xenoturbella is generally described as having a very simple body (interpreted by many as primitively simple), its genome is of a similar complexity to many other bilaterians, perhaps lending support to the idea that the simplicity of X. bocki is derived.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comprehensive genomic analysis.
